Whereunto
hwâr-un-tōo'
adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew 'asher... shammah, Greek eis ho)
A compound of where and unto, meaning to which or unto what. It is the fuller and older form answering to thereunto, and in the epistles it becomes a word of vocation — the end to which a man is called and toward which he labours.

Biblical Definition

Whereunto means to which, and in the New Testament it repeatedly marks a calling and its object. Paul charges Timothy: “Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses” (1 Timothy 6:12). Eternal life is not merely offered but is the end to which the man was called, and the fight is the taking hold of what God has already appointed. Of his own ministry he says, “Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily” (Colossians 1:29) — a sentence that holds together the hardest human effort and the divine energy producing it, which is the Reformed account of sanctification in miniature. The word also frames the Lord's search for a fit comparison: “Whereunto then shall I liken the men of this generation?” (Luke 7:31). And the psalmist uses it of God as a place of continual return: “Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort” (Psalm 71:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

A compound adverb meaning to which or unto what. In Scripture it names the end to which a man is called — eternal life, whereunto thou art also called — and the labour undertaken toward it.

expand to see more

WHEREUNTO, adv. [where and unto.] To which; unto which; to what end.

2. Interrogatively, to what? as, whereunto shall I liken it?

3. It is the fuller form of whereto, and answers to thereunto, which refers backward.

4. It is retained chiefly in the scriptural and formal style.

5. In Scripture, eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, 1 Tim. 6; Whereunto I also labour, Col. 1.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 6:12 — "Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses."

Acts 13:2 — "As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them."

Psalm 71:3 — "Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress."

Luke 7:31 — "And the Lord said, Whereunto then shall I liken the men of this generation? and to what are they like?"

Modern Corruption

Calling has been thinned into career language — a personal sense of fit, a passion to be followed. In Scripture the calling is God's act with an object He has named, and the believer's part is to lay hold of what he was called to.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is effectual calling as God's work. In the New Testament the called are those whom God has summoned out of darkness, and the calling is according to His purpose and grace, given in Christ before the world began. Vocation in the Reformation sense then follows: because God has called a man to Himself, the ordinary work of his hands is service rendered to God and not a lesser thing than ministry. Luther and the Puritans recovered exactly this against a medieval scheme that reserved vocation for monks and priests.

Colossians 1:29 keeps the balance the doctrine needs. Paul labours — the verb is one of agony and exhaustion — and he labours according to his working, which worketh in me mightily. Sanctification is neither passive waiting nor unaided effort. It is real striving, empowered by real grace, and the same apostle who says work out your own salvation with fear and trembling gives the reason in the next breath: for it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. A calling in Scripture always comes with the power to pursue it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew expresses whereunto with the relative 'asher and a directional suffix; Greek uses eis ho or the dative of the relative. The vocabulary of calling — kaleo, klesis — governs the New Testament texts.

expand to see more

Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call, to summon, to name; the verb of God's effectual calling.

Greek klesis (G2821) — a calling or invitation; the noun for the vocation to which believers are summoned.

Greek agonizomai (G75) — to strive as in a contest, to agonize; Paul's labour in Colossians 1:29.

Greek energeia (G1753) — working, operative power; the divine energy at work in that labour.

Hebrew ma'on (H4583) — a habitation or dwelling; the strong habitation of Psalm 71:3.

Usage

"Of the end to which a believer is called: eternal life, whereunto thou art also called (1 Timothy 6:12)."

"Of labour empowered by God's own working: Whereunto I also labour, striving according to his working (Colossians 1:29)."

"Of God as a refuge continually returned to: Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort (Psalm 71:3)."
